**Conclusion:**  
No. An employer may not count the cost of required uniforms toward the statutory credit for meals, lodging, or other facilities. Uniform costs are treated separately under the uniform‑payment rules and are not included in the meal‑ or lodging‑credit provisions.

**Supporting regulations**

1. **Uniform costs are a distinct business expense** – The Davis‑Bacon Act uniform rule requires the employer to furnish uniforms at no charge to employees or to reimburse them at the prescribed rate; it does not allow those costs to be applied as a credit for meals, lodging, or other facilities. [29 CFR Part 4 § 4.168]  

2. **Meal and lodging credits are limited to those specific items** – The credit provisions for breakfast, lunch, dinner, and lodging specify the maximum percentages of the minimum hourly wage that may be credited, and they refer only to the actual cost or fair value of furnishing meals or lodging. [29 CFR Part 552 § 552.100]  

3. **“Other facilities” for credit purposes do not include uniforms** – The definition of “other facilities” (e.g., meals, dormitory rooms, tuition, merchandise, housing, transportation) does not list uniforms, and the regulations governing board, lodging, or other facilities focus on items customarily furnished to employees, not employer‑required uniforms. [29 CFR Part 541 § 541.606]  

4. **Uniforms are identified as a cost primarily for employer convenience** – While uniforms appear in a list of facilities primarily benefiting the employer, this classification does not make them eligible for the meal‑ or lodging‑credit calculations. [29 CFR Part 531 § 531.3(2)]  

Therefore, the cost of required uniforms cannot be used to satisfy or reduce the employer’s credit for food, lodging, or other facilities under the applicable wage‑determination rules.

answer:
An employer’s violation of the child‑labor provisions (section 12 or section 13(c) of the FLSA) is deemed **willful** when the employer **knew** that the conduct was prohibited **or** acted with **reckless disregard** of the Act’s requirements, with all surrounding facts and circumstances taken into account. Receipt of advice from a Wage‑and‑Hour Division official that the conduct is unlawful can be evidence that the employer’s conduct was “knowing,” but it does not by itself determine willfulness. Reckless disregard includes a failure to make further inquiry that a reasonable employer should have made to determine compliance. [29 CFR Part 579 § 579.2] (current regulation)  

- The definition states that a violation of section 12 or 13(c) “shall be deemed to be willful … where the employer knew that its conduct was prohibited by the Act or showed reckless disregard for the requirements of the Act.” [29 CFR Part 579 § 579.2]  
- It adds that “All of the facts and circumstances surrounding the violation shall be taken into account in determining whether a violation was willful.” [29 CFR Part 579 § 579.2]  
- It notes that “the employer’s receipt of advice … can be sufficient to show that the employer’s conduct is knowing, but is not automatically dispositive.” [29 CFR Part 579 § 579.2]  
- “Reckless disregard … means … the employer should have inquired further … and failed to make adequate further inquiry.” [29 CFR Part 579 § 579.2]  

Thus, a child‑labor violation is considered willful when the employer either knew it was illegal or acted with reckless disregard, evaluated in light of all relevant facts, and advice from officials may support a finding of knowledge but does not alone establish willfulness.

- The regulation that governs the interaction of FMLA with the FLSA states that providing unpaid FMLA‑qualifying leave to a salaried executive, administrative, professional, or computer employee “will not cause the employee to lose the FLSA exemption” and that the employer “may make deductions from the employee’s salary for any hours taken as intermittent or reduced FMLA leave… without affecting the exempt status of the employee” (29 CFR Part 825 § 825.206(a)).  
- The salary‑basis rule itself permits an employer to withhold a proportionate part of the full salary for weeks in which an exempt employee takes unpaid FMLA leave (29 CFR Part 541 § 541.602(7)).  
- The special exception applies only to employees who are eligible for FMLA leave and only to leave that qualifies as FMLA leave; deductions for non‑FMLA leave could affect exemption status (29 CFR Part 825 § 825.206(c)).  

Therefore, when the leave is bona‑fide unpaid FMLA leave and the employee meets the FMLA eligibility requirements, the employer can deduct the corresponding pay without jeopardizing the employee’s overtime exemption.

The core FMLA eligibility requirement that an employee must have worked at least 1,250 hours in the 12 months before leave has **not been changed** since the law was enacted in 1993. **Conclusion:** Federal regulations do not impose a universal minimum number of paid‑vacation days on employers. The amount of vacation that must be provided is set by the specific fringe‑benefit determination that applies to a contract, and a common provision is one week (40 hours) of paid vacation after an employee has completed one year of service, unless the determination says otherwise.  

**Supporting rules**

- The regulation governing vacation fringe benefits states that an employee “who renders the ‘one year of service’ continuously becomes eligible for the ‘one week paid vacation’ (i.e., 40 hours of paid vacation, unless otherwise specified in an applicable wage determination)” on the anniversary of employment and each subsequent anniversary. It also makes clear that no vacation accrues before the anniversary and that any fraction of a week is only provided if the particular wage determination expressly provides it【29 CFR Part 4 § 4.173】.  

- Because the rule ties the vacation entitlement to what is “specified in an applicable wage determination,” there is no blanket statutory or regulatory minimum of vacation days for all employers; the required amount can vary from contract to contract【29 CFR Part 4 § 4.173】.  

- An example in the health‑welfare provision shows that an employee “entitled to two weeks paid vacation who instead works the full 52 weeks … would be due an extra 80 hours of vacation pay in lieu of actually taking the vacation,” but this example assumes the employee already has a two‑week vacation entitlement under the applicable determination; it does not create a universal two‑week requirement【29 CFR Part 4 § 4.175】.  

Therefore, federal law does not mandate a specific number of paid‑vacation days across the board; the entitlement is determined by the contract‑specific fringe‑benefit determination, with a typical baseline of one week after one year of service.

answer:
You do not get a paid “lunch break” when you eat at your desk while continuing to answer phones; that time must be counted as work time and paid.

**Why**

* A bona‑fide meal period is **not** work time only if the employee is completely relieved of all duties while eating.  If the employee is required to perform any duties—active or inactive—while eating, the period is not a bona‑fide meal period and must be treated as work time.  (29 CFR Part 785 § 785.19(a)).

* Eating at your desk and still answering phones means you are not completely relieved from duty; you are performing work while you eat. Therefore the time is not a bona‑fide meal period and must be compensated as hours worked. (29 CFR Part 785 § 785.19(a))

* Even when an employee is “on duty” for less than 24 hours, the time is considered work time regardless of sleeping or personal activities, because the employee’s time is given to the employer. (29 CFR Part 785 § 785.21) This reinforces that any period during which you are still answering phones is work time. 

**Result:** The lunch time you spend at your desk answering phones is not an unpaid meal break; it must be paid as regular work time.

answer:
**Conclusion:**  
If your employer requires you to attend training, the time is normally compensable — you must be paid for it even when the training is scheduled after your regular workday. The only situations where such after‑hours training is not compensable are the narrow exceptions that apply to employees of state or local governments who attend certain legally‑required certification training outside regular hours. Independent training you take on your own initiative is not compensable.

**Supporting rules**

* The general rule is that “time spent in attending training required by an employer is normally considered compensable hours of work” [29 CFR Part 553 § 553.226(a)].  

* The regulation lists limited non‑compensable exceptions that apply **only to employees of state and local governments** who attend required certification training outside regular working hours (paragraphs (b)(1)–(b)(3)) [29 CFR Part 553 § 553.226(b)].  

* Police or fire‑protection employees who are free to use off‑class time for personal pursuits are also not compensated for that free time [29 CFR Part 553 § 553.226(c)].  

* Training that you attend on your own initiative after hours (independent schooling) is expressly not “hours worked” for the employer [29 CFR Part 785 § 785.30].  

* The Act requires that wages, including compensation for such training time, be paid promptly (no later than the next regular payday) [29 CFR Part 4 § 4.165(a)(1)].  

Therefore, unless you fall within one of the specific government‑employee exceptions, your employer must pay you for mandatory training that occurs after your normal work hours.

No. An ordinary one‑hour drive from home to the office is not required to be counted as paid work time.  

- The Portal‑to‑Portal Act expressly excludes “ordinary travel from home to work” from the definition of hours worked, even if the employer agrees to pay for it【29 CFR Part 785 § 785.34】.  
- Travel that is part of the day’s principal activity (e.g., moving between job sites) must be counted as work time, but a commute that begins at home and ends at the employer’s premises is treated as “home‑to‑work” travel and is not compensable【29 CFR Part 785 § 785.38】.  
- Only when the travel is for a special assignment or otherwise “integral to the principal activity” (such as the scenario in § 785.37) could it be considered work time; a regular daily commute does not meet that condition.  

Therefore, under the current regulations, your daily one‑hour drive to the office is not payable work time unless a specific contract, custom, or practice makes it compensable, which the Portal‑to‑Portal Act still allows to be excluded.

answer:
**Conclusion:**  
A private employer generally cannot require you to take a lie‑detector (polygraph) test. Only very limited exemptions exist—such as an employer‑initiated investigation of theft or other economic loss that meets strict conditions, or a federal‑government‑related national‑defense/security situation. If none of those exemptions apply, the employer’s request is prohibited.  

**Supporting rules**

1. **General prohibition** – Covered (private) employers are barred from “requiring, requesting, suggesting or causing… any employee… to take or submit to a lie detector test” (29 CFR § 801.4(a)(1)). [29 CFR Part 801 § 801.4]  

2. **Exemption for economic‑loss investigations** – A private employer may request a polygraph only when it is conducting an *ongoing* investigation of economic loss or injury (e.g., theft, embezzlement) and the employer meets all of the detailed conditions listed in § 801.12(a) (reasonable suspicion, employee access, written statement, etc.) [29 CFR Part 801 § 801.12]  

3. **Exemption for federal national‑defense/security work** – The limited exemptions in § 801.11 apply **only to the Federal Government** and do not permit private employers to administer such tests. [29 CFR Part 801 § 801.11]  

4. **Scope of the Act** – EPPA “prohibits most private employers… from using any lie detector tests” (except the narrow exemptions above). [29 CFR Part 801 § 801.1]  

5. **State or collective‑bargaining protections** – State laws or collective‑bargaining agreements that are more restrictive than EPPA also forbid the test, and they are not pre‑empted. [29 CFR Part 801 § 801.5(a)]

**Therefore**, unless your employer falls within one of the narrow exemptions (economic‑loss investigation meeting all statutory requirements, or a federal‑government/defense context), it cannot legally force you to take a lie‑detector test.

Overtime must be paid at **least** one‑and‑a‑half times the employee’s regular rate, but it can be higher—employers may pay double‑time or any other greater amount if they choose.  

- The Fair Labor Standards Act requires overtime compensation “not less than one and one‑half times the regular rate” and allows the overtime rate to be “greater than the regular rate… such as one and one‑third, one and one‑half or two times that rate” (i.e., double time)【29 CFR Part 778 § 778.308】.  
- When an employee works two different jobs, the overtime rate “not less than one and one‑half times the hourly non‑overtime rate” is required, but the regulation does not prohibit a higher rate such as double time【29 CFR Part 778 § 778.419】.  

Therefore, overtime is **time‑and‑a‑half as the minimum legal rate**, and **double time is permissible but not required**.

answer:
**Conclusion:**  
Employers must keep most required records for **at least three years**, but some supplementary or special‑purpose records may be kept for a shorter period (typically **two years**), and a few specific forms require a longer period (e.g., OSHA 200/101 forms for **five years**).

**Supporting rules**

* General payroll, certificates, collective‑bargaining agreements, and other basic records must be retained for three years.  
  * “Each employer shall preserve for at least 3 years… payroll records… certificates, agreements, plans, notices, etc.” [29 CFR Part 516 § 516.5]  

* Basic records (payroll, certificates, employment agreements) are required to be kept for three years, while supplementary records (time‑cards, wage‑rate tables, shipping/billing records, etc.) need only be kept for two years.  
  * “Basic records… must be preserved for at least 3 years. Supplementary records… need be preserved for only 2 years.” [29 CFR Part 779 § 779.514]  

* The regulation that lists the supplementary basic records explicitly sets a two‑year retention period.  
  * “Each employer… shall preserve for a period of at least 2 years… (1) Basic employment and earnings records… (2) Wage rate tables.” [29 CFR Part 516 § 516.6]  

* Records related to polygraph examinations under the Act must be kept for three years from the date of the examination (or request).  
  * “The following records shall be kept for a minimum period of three years from the date the polygraph examination is conducted…” [29 CFR Part 801 § 801.30]  

* Contractors and subcontractors under the Service Contract Act must retain required employment records for three years after the work is completed.  
  * “They are required to be maintained for 3 years from the completion of the work…” [29 CFR Part 4 § 4.185]  

* OSHA 200 and 101 injury/illness forms must be saved for five years after the year to which they relate.  
  * “You must save your copies of the OSHA 200 and 101 forms for five years following the year to which they relate…” [29 CFR Part 1904 § 1904.44]  

* Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) records must be kept for no less than three years and be available for inspection.  
  * “Employers must keep the records specified by these regulations for no less than three years and make them available for inspection…” [29 CFR Part 825 § 825.500]  

**Summary:**  
- **3‑year rule** applies to most payroll, certification, agreement, and polygraph‑related records, as well as Service Contract Act records and FMLA records.  
- **2‑year rule** applies to supplementary records such as time‑cards, wage‑rate tables, and shipping/billing documents.  
- **5‑year rule** applies specifically to OSHA 200/101 forms.

**Conclusion:** Your tips belong to you, not to your employer. An employer may not keep or use your tips except as a credit toward its minimum‑wage obligation or as part of a lawful tip pool that includes only employees who regularly receive tips. 

**Supporting rules**

- A tip is defined as a customer‑provided gratuity that is the property of the employee, and an employer may use tips only “as a credit against its minimum‑wage obligations to the employee, or in furtherance of a tip pool limited to employees who customarily and regularly receive tips” [29 CFR Part 531 § 531.52 (a)].

- Even when an employer takes a tip credit, it is prohibited from using employees’ tips for any other purpose [29 CFR Part 531 § 531.52 (b)].

- Managers and supervisors may not keep any portion of an employee’s tips (unless the tip is directly received for their own service) [29 CFR Part 531 § 531.52 (2)].

- Section 3(m)(2)(B) of the Act expressly bars an employer from keeping tips received by its employees for any purpose [29 CFR Part 531 § 531.50 (c)].

- The 2011 final rule reiterates that “tips are the property of the employee whether or not the employer has taken a tip credit” and that the employer is prohibited from using tips except as a credit or a valid tip pool [FR Doc. 2011‑6749 (Final rule) § 531.52].

These provisions make clear that your tips are yours, not your employer’s.
